newsitem.title: USA: Mass. tax committee begins laying levies low.
newsitem.headline: Mass. tax committee begins laying levies low.

text.p: The Massachusetts Taxation Committee moved on several major bills, approving the cancellation of the sales tax on Internet services and beginning the process of approving a controversial new tax on home sales, State House News reported.

The committee members in attendance at Wednesday's session voted 7-4 in favor of a bill that will let communities on Cape Cod impose a 1 percent tax on home sales, to be paid by the seller. The original version of the bill imposed the tax on the buyer. The first $100,000 of value would be exempt from the new levy.
The tax would have to be approved by Barnstable County voters in a binding referendum.

Proponents of the transfer tax say it would raise money for open space preservation on the environmentally sensitive Cape, where communities struggle against growth pressures and the fiscal constraints of Proposition 2-1/2.

Opponents say the state does not need a new sales tax, particularly one that stands in the way of the dream of home ownership. Rep. Ronald Gauch (R-Shrewsbury) said the measure would have the Legislature "start down the slippery slope of circumventing Prop. 2 1/2," which is supposed to limit the burden property taxes impose on Massachusetts families.
The committee will be polled over the next few days to obtain a vote of all 17 members, but Senate Chairman Warren Tolman (D-Watertown) said it will win approval.

Tolman voted against another transfer-tax bill filed by the Cambridge City Council, on which the committee will also be polled. It would impose a 1 percent tax on the value of any home sale, with the first $300,000 of value exempt.
Tolman said he voted against the Cambridge bill because it imposes the tax on the buyer instead of the seller.

The committee approved a bill that would continue the imposition of the state's 5 percent sales tax on telephone calls, but stipulate that Internet Service Providers would be exempt from the sales tax.
The Department of Revenue has been attempting to make ISPs pay sales taxes on their service delivery retroactively as well as going forward.
The bill sent out of committee stipulates the ISPs have been exempt from charging their customers that tax since Jan. 1, 1990.
"We think it's important that we allow ISPs to continue to operate profitably in Massachusetts and not have to worry about this," Tolman said.
